source.title: On the Learning Dynamics of Deep Neural Networks
source.citation: Rémi Tachet Des Combes et al., 2018
source.authors: Rémi Tachet Des Combes; M. Pezeshki; S. Shabanian; Aaron C. Courville; Yoshua Bengio

page_placements.theme: Transfer and distribution shift depend on feature relevance and coverage

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and appendices; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports that gradient descent can favor frequent features and fail to learn rare informative features, but its experiment measures transfer to an untouched test distribution rather than the listed same-distribution generalization versions.
record.gate_note: The paper’s theoretical learning curves and hinge-loss comparison concern training dynamics, not the listed generalization claims. Its cats-and-dogs experiment reports results on modified and untouched test data; that distribution-shift result does not test the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study investigates learning dynamics and gradient starvation, but its results do not test V1–V8. Its cats-and-dogs experiment measures transfer after introducing a discriminative brightness cue; it supplies none of the comparisons required by the listed versions. The proposed generalization mechanism does not contradict any version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors propose gradient starvation as a possible explanation for generalization: prioritizing frequent features may suppress individual-example idiosyncrasies, while also hindering learning of rare informative features and transfer to other distributions. Its generalization benefit is suggested, rather than directly demonstrated.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies simplified binary-classification learning dynamics and a feature-frequency experiment; it does not reproduce the methods or measurements in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature frequency is varied in the theoretical analysis; the image experiment imposes a highly discriminative brightness feature. The paper does not report a same-distribution generalization-gap comparison across these conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: A VGG16-like classifier trained with a class-specific brightness cue achieves 100% accuracy on modified training and test images but 43.2% on untouched test images.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An imposed discriminative shortcut can support perfect performance within the modified distribution while failing to transfer to untouched images.

fits_no_version.finding: Under restrictive binary-classification assumptions, Theorem 6.1 bounds confidence on an informative rare feature presented alone, despite high confidence on training examples containing the frequent feature.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning a frequent informative feature can suppress learning of a less frequent informative feature and impair transfer when the frequent feature is absent.

record.problems: The main theoretical analysis relies on strong assumptions, including linear separability and highly simplified data. The image experiment uses a hand-crafted brightness cue and reports no uncertainty estimates or control comparison.
record.rows_left_out: Theoretical bounds and plotted curves in Sections 3–6 concern simplified learning dynamics or feature confidence, not the listed versions’ same-distribution generalization claims. No rows were omitted for a tested version.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label fitting and natural-label generalization under the same architecture and recipe, including chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Test-error changes when width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification performance and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD held-out performance under limited or broader tuning, weight-decay changes, or optimizer switching.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recovery through recipe changes or longer training.
Effects of adding or removing dropout and weight decay across training-set sizes and augmentation conditions.
Association of magnitude-aware sharpness with generalization gaps and comparisons with norm- or margin-based measures.
Test-accuracy effects of removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: T5 is unwarranted because neither the theoretical argument nor the experiment establishes that a listed version is wrong or incomplete. Row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8; the reported accuracies themselves are readable and verified in Table 2.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of random-label and natural-label generalization.
No network-width sweep or test-error measurement beyond interpolation.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No comparison of adaptive optimizers with SGD on held-out performance.
No sharpness or other generalization-measure comparison.
No removal or retraining of memorized examples.

rows.subject: classifier with an architecture similar to VGG16
rows.operation_detail: Trained on cats-and-dogs images modified by setting cat pixels to 0–127 and dog pixels to 128–255; no regularization was applied.
rows.note: This is a result on the deliberately modified dataset; the paper does not report random-label fitting.
rows.check: The 100% modified-data training accuracy is correctly recorded, but it cannot establish any listed version. No random-label comparison is reported.

relation.reason: The introduction, related work and discussion consider generalization and memorization, but the study neither tests a listed version nor uses its finding as a tool.

tranche.reason: The learning-dynamics analysis and brightness-cue experiment address related mechanisms but supply none of the comparisons required by V1–V8.

source_check.notes: The proposed generalization benefit of gradient starvation is conjectural; the experiment demonstrates poor transfer after introducing a brightness cue. Appendix E.2 reverses the brightness adjectives in one sentence, but its explicit pixel ranges agree with Section 6 and R1.
